episodes.title: What Jensen Huang's Stunning Return Means for the AI Trade
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Odd Lots runs an emergency pod on the whiplash AI trade: S&P 500 entered a correction Friday (worst week since COVID, -7%), then Nvidia's Jensen Huang was reinstated and stocks ripped higher Monday (Nasdaq 100 +6.9%). Barclays' Alexander Altmann argues this is less dead-cat-bounce and more a high-vol regime where both up and down moves are amplified, with the Fed's financial-conditions tightening as the key forward risk.

**Key points**
- VIX hit 40 intraday Friday, still around 30 Monday — consistent with ~2% daily S&P swings continuing.
- Fastest one-month tightening of financial conditions since Dec 2018, comparable to March 2020; roughly 3.5 Fed hikes now priced over the next year, with Dec 9 meeting seen as near-certain (odds eased slightly from >100% to 91% late last week).
- Friday's selloff was technical: ~$35bn levered ETF selling, 58th-worst S&P liquidity day in 10 years, dealer short-gamma around the 7100 strike amplifying the slide; no safe-haven bid (Bitcoin, gold, Treasuries all weak).
- Semiconductor valuations reset sharply (30-40% cut to forward capex expectations); credit spreads on hyperscaler/data-center/neocloud debt have not tightened, signaling a higher AI financing cost environment.
- Oil below $80 and largely ignored despite Iran/Strait-of-Hormuz risk; Anthropic's Rimann-hypothesis claim also dismissed as not yet monetizable.

**FX / rates implications**
- A Fed pivot toward 50bp-style hawkishness or continued financial-conditions tightening (per Waller/Barr/Hammack commentary) would pressure global risk assets and could support USD/DXY broadly, a headwind for EM Asia and LatAm carry trades.
- Credit spread widening in US hyperscaler/data-center debt is an early-warning indicator for broader risk-off spillover into EM credit and FX.
- No direct EM Asia/LatAm currency commentary, but the risk-on/risk-off whiplash in US equities and vol (VIX) is a key global risk-sentiment driver for EM FX positioning.

**Watch list**
- FOMC meeting December 9 — hike probability and messaging on further tightening.
- Credit spreads on data-center/neocloud/hyperscaler bonds for AI financing stress signals.
- VIX level as a proxy for continued large bidirectional swings in global risk assets.

episodes.title: How Hedge Funds Are Navigating Stock Market Volatility
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Goldman Sachs' prime brokerage co-head Vincent Lin details how hedge funds de-grossed risk over the prior several weeks before pivoting last week to adding outright shorts, reflecting fragile sentiment amid an AI-driven equity drawdown. The dynamics matter for macro traders as a read on global risk appetite, positioning extremes and upcoming US data that will shape the Fed's policy path into year-end.

**Key points**
- Hedge funds added ETF shorts up 19 percentage points in the past week, the third-largest weekly increase in a decade, after weeks of de-grossing.
- Rotation into defensive sectors (consumer staples, utilities, REITs) and away from tech/AI infrastructure; shorts concentrated in rate-sensitive consumer names like homebuilders.
- "Fast money" (hedge funds, CTAs) positioning near multi-year lows, while "slow money" (401k/mutual funds) remains elevated — $150bn of ETF/mutual fund inflows in the past month despite the selloff.
- Fundamental long/short funds up ~7% YTD after giving back gains from a 17% mid-year peak; systematic/quant equity strategies have strengthened since mid-year.
- AI narrative seen transitioning from infrastructure buildout to monetization, historically the hardest phase of a tech cycle, pressuring sentiment and risk appetite.

**FX / rates implications**
- Persistent de-grossing and defensive positioning signal fragile global risk sentiment, a headwind for high-beta EM FX (IDR, ZAR-type, BRL) and supportive of USD/DXY on safe-haven flows if equity weakness persists.
- Elevated "slow money" equity exposure despite a selloff suggests downside risk if household flows reverse, which would amplify risk-off pressure on EM carry trades.
- Low CTA/momentum positioning near multi-year lows implies reduced systematic selling pressure going forward if prices stabilize — a mild tailwind for risk assets and EM carry.

**Watch list**
- US PCE data later this week, payrolls next week, and November CPI in three weeks — key inputs for whether the Fed's recent hawkish posture holds or reverses, directly relevant to USD and UST yield trajectory.
- Mega-cap/hyperscaler earnings this week for AI capex signals.
- Credit spread behavior as a leading indicator hedge fund clients are monitoring for further de-risking triggers.

episodes.title: Global Rates : 2027 Outlook Themes for European Rates
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
JPMorgan's European rate strategists lay out 2027 outlook themes for Euro and Sterling rates, covering ECB/BoE policy paths, German duration, France/EU spreads, swap curves, and UK politics. Relevant mainly as a DM rates read-through that shapes global risk appetite, term-premium dynamics and USD/UST cross-currents that spill into EM.

**Key points**
- ECB expected to deliver two more 25bp hikes (December, March 2027) to 3%, then hold; forward reds/greens seen 10-15bp cheap to fair value.
- ECB balance sheet (QE runoff) becomes a bigger theme in H2 2027 as excess liquidity falls toward ~€1.5tn; options include lending ops, TLTROs or a structural bond portfolio.
- German 10y Bund targeted at 3.05% by mid-2027, 2.90% by end-2027; constructive on German duration vs US.
- France-Germany 10y spread forecast ~110bp mid-2027, 90bp end-2027, with French presidential election as main volatility source; EU-Germany spread seen at 95bp/90bp.
- BoE hiked to 4% in November; base case one more 25bp hike (Feb, to 4.25%) then hold, though market prices ~3 more hikes - seen as excessive; UK 10y yields above 5% viewed as compelling for duration.
- UK political risk: ~30-40% chance of an early election by end-2027 amid rising Reform/Conservative poll support, a potential source of fiscal term-premium and gilt curve steepening.

**FX / rates implications**
- Further ECB/BoE tightening and still-elevated UST yields keep global term premia and DM rates volatility elevated, a headwind for EM carry trades and a modest USD/DXY support factor via relative rate differentials.
- French political risk and any OAT spread blowout could trigger broader European risk-off, historically a drag on EM risk sentiment and EM FX via global risk channels.
- A disorderly UST sell-off is flagged as the main external risk to European duration calls - relevant for EM rates as UST moves remain the dominant global anchor for EM local yields.

**Watch list**
- ECB meetings in December 2026 and March 2027 for the final hiking moves.
- French presidential election and second-round dynamics in 2027 as the key OAT spread catalyst.
- BoE's February 2027 meeting and any signs of an early UK general election call in H2 2027.
- ECB balance sheet/liquidity communication expected to intensify in H2 2027 as reserves approach €1.5tn.

episodes.title: NVIDIA Reversal, AI Risks and Retail Resilience
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
This episode is a US equity-market-focused show covering a sharp reversal in Nvidia and AI-complex stocks, Washington policy risk around Jensen Huang's reinstatement, a bullish S&P 500 call to 10,000, and a JPMorgan economist's forecast for three Fed rate hikes starting next month. It is primarily US-centric with no direct EM Asia or LATAM discussion, but the Fed-hike call and risk-sentiment swings carry indirect read-through for global macro.

**Key points**
- Nvidia fell ~7% after yesterday's 32% gain; Nasdaq down 1.3%; AI-complex names (CoreWeave -12%, AMD -9%, Micron -10%) also reversed.
- Congress (both parties) is moving toward new tech/chip export restrictions (Match Act, AI Overwatch Act, Chip Security Act) that could extend US semi-cap equipment curbs to allies like Netherlands and Japan.
- JPMorgan's Bruce Kasman forecasts three straight 25bp Fed rate hikes starting next month, citing persistent inflation, tight labor markets, and job growth above 100,000/month; does not expect a 50bp hike.
- Federated Hermes' Stephen DeNichilo sees S&P 500 reaching 10,000 by end of next year (~40% upside), citing resilient consumer, strong corporate profits, and historical post-midterm seasonality.
- Consumer confidence surged in November to a nearly two-year high; strong retail earnings (Dollar Tree, Best Buy, Dick's) ahead of Black Friday.

**FX / rates implications**
- A Fed that hikes three times starting next month (vs. market expectations of cuts/pause) would be USD-supportive and UST-yield-bearish, tightening financial conditions globally and pressuring EM carry trades and EM FX broadly via higher US real rates.
- Renewed US-China chip export restriction risk (Match Act scope creep to allies) adds to trade/tariff-related tension that could weigh on CNY/CNH and broader Asia FX sentiment if tech supply chains are disrupted.
- Equity risk-off in AI/tech (Nasdaq -1.3%) alongside a Dow that stayed green suggests a rotational rather than broad risk-off move, limiting spillover to EM for now.

**Watch list**
- Next FOMC meeting in two weeks — Kasman does not expect a 50bp move but flags hikes at the next three meetings.
- December 11th government funding deadline, tied to defense authorization bill and potential chip-restriction legislation.
- Congressional hearings on Nvidia/Jensen Huang expected to continue into January-February 2027.

episodes.title: Sorry, even store brands are expensive now
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
This Planet Money/Indicator episode introduces "cheapflation," a phenomenon where cheaper, budget-brand groceries have risen in price faster than premium brands during the COVID-era inflation surge. The finding, based on a 2024 academic paper, has implications for how inflation inequality is measured and understood, but is a US consumer-economics story with no direct market or EM transmission.

**Key points**
- Harvard Business School economist Alberto Cavallo and a Bank of Canada co-author studied price data for over 2 million products across 10 countries (including US, Netherlands, Argentina) from 2018 to May 2024.
- In the US, cheap food/beverage prices rose 30% from January 2020 to May 2024, versus 22% for premium versions; in Italy, cheap goods rose almost 30% versus 15% for premium.
- They found no meaningful evidence of "shrinkflation" (smaller packages, same price) in the dataset, pivoting instead to this price-tier divergence.
- Drivers: demand-side shift by shoppers toward cheaper brands pushes those prices up, while thin profit margins on budget products mean producers pass through cost increases (including tariffs) faster than premium-brand makers.
- Cavallo argues cheapflation may have eroded the real benefit of COVID-era government stimulus payments for low-income households, a consideration for policymakers assessing subsidy adequacy.
- Anecdotal detail: a can of corn that once cost 33 cents now costs close to $1; egg prices have recently come down.

**FX / rates implications**
None directly — this is a microeconomic/consumer-inflation-measurement story about US and other DM grocery pricing, not a driver of EM FX, rates, or global risk sentiment.

**Watch list**
- US CPI/PCE components for food-at-home disaggregated by price tier, if available, to track cheapflation dynamics.
- Broader narrative on US affordability as a political issue following recent midterm elections, which could feed into fiscal/subsidy policy debates relevant to consumption-driven growth forecasts.

episodes.title: Global Rates: DM inflation - Rinse and repeat
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
JPMorgan's Global Rates team lays out a 2027 DM inflation outlook titled "rinse and repeat," arguing next year looks like this year: front-end breakevens track energy, five-year-five-year inflation stays range-bound, and real yields rise with policy tightening. The standout call is a Fed seen hiking three times (December, January, March) because core PCE has run 88bp above core CPI — the widest gap since the Fed began PCE targeting — even as core CPI fell to 2.4%.

**Key points**
- Market-implied Fed terminal rate rose ~125bp this year; US 10y and 1y1y real yields up 70-150bp as Fed/ECB hiked.
- Commodity prices explain 44% of 2026 breakeven variation but under 8% of forward (3-month-lag-adjusted) inflation pricing — a historical break, reflecting energy backwardation and a Fed leaning against pass-through.
- Tariffs seen adding 0.1-0.2 to core CPI, mostly in the first six months; JPM's commodity desk expects crude near/below $70 in 2027.
- 46% of institutional clients now expect core CPI below 2.5% over 2-5 years, up from 28% last year.
- Eurozone headline HICP seen peaking 4.1% in December, falling to 1.6% by end-2027; core sticky 2.7-2.8%; assumes Brent to $75 and TTF gas to ~€45/MWh by spring.
- UK: October headline CPI 3.6%, core 2.8%, services 3.7%; BoE's next 25bp hike pushed to February from December; headline seen peaking 4.2% in February, RPI peaking 6%.
- French OAT-Bund spread widened ~90bp in late October on political risk; linker supply rising to €65bn in 2027.

**FX / rates implications**
- A Fed hiking three more times through March is a direct USD-positive, UST-yield-positive signal that tightens global financial conditions and pressures EM carry trades, FX and local rates broadly — watch EM Asia/LATAM central banks' reaction function if DXY and UST yields extend higher.
- Narrowing inflation risk premium and fairly-valued US breakevens suggest less upside surprise risk for US real yields, a moderating but still-firm USD backdrop for EM.
- Lower Brent ($70-75 base case) is a tailwind for EM oil importers (India, Philippines, Indonesia) but a headwind for LATAM oil exporters (Mexico, Colombia).
- ECB/BoE policy paths staying inflation-anchored but cautious keep EUR/GBP rate differentials versus USD in focus for broad risk sentiment.

**Watch list**
- FOMC meetings: December, January, March — key for USD/UST trajectory.
- Crude oil path toward JPM's ~$70 2027 forecast.
- French political/fiscal headlines and OAT-Bund spread, French elections next year.
- BoE February meeting (next hike) and UK CPI/RPI trajectory toward 4%+ in H1 2027.
